title: UX Is Thankless (That's Good)
intro: Good UX is invisible. That's not a failure of recognition — it's proof the work is doing its job. Understanding hedonic adaptation changes how you measure your own impact.

learn.title: Hedonic adaptation and UX
learn.text:
**Hedonic adaptation** is the psychological tendency to return to a baseline level of satisfaction after changes — positive or negative.

In UX, this means: **every improvement you ship becomes the new normal.** Users don't keep feeling grateful for a fix. They just stop noticing the problem.

This creates a paradox: the better your UX work is, the more invisible it becomes. Users don't thank you for things that "just work." They only notice when things break.

This isn't a bug — it's the nature of good infrastructure.

try.q: Your team fixed a confusing settings page 6 months ago. Support tickets dropped 40%. Now nobody mentions it. What happened?
options: Hedonic adaptation
Users found a workaround
The fix wasn't that important
Users forgot the old version
try.explain: Hedonic adaptation: the improvement became the new normal. The 40% ticket drop is your proof of impact. (The fix became invisible baseline.)

learn.title: Measuring invisible impact
learn.text:
If good UX is invisible, how do you prove your work matters? Track **what stopped happening**:

→ Support tickets that disappeared
→ Error rates that dropped
→ Task completion time that shortened
→ Abandonment rates that fell
→ Training requests that went away

These "absence metrics" are your strongest evidence. Nobody notices when the plumbing works — but the plumber can show you the water bill.

Document your **before** numbers obsessively. You can't show improvement without a baseline.

try.q: You want to prove impact of a checkout redesign. What's your strongest argument?
options: Completion rate went from 62% to 84%
The design team is proud of it
Stakeholders approved the new design
It follows current design trends
try.explain: Numbers that show a change in behavior are your strongest evidence. Opinions fade; data persists.

learn.title: Reframing "thankless" as success
learn.text:
The absence of praise is the **presence of usability**. Reframe your expectations:

**Bad UX** gets attention → complaints, workarounds, support tickets
**Good UX** gets silence → "it just works"

This means your job security comes from a paradox: the better you are, the harder it is to see why you're needed.

The fix isn't to make your work more visible by adding unnecessary features or friction. It's to:
→ **Document baselines** before every project
→ **Track absence metrics** after shipping
→ **Communicate in business language** — cost saved, revenue retained, time recovered
→ **Build a portfolio of before/after data**, not just pretty screens

try.q: A VP asks: "What has the UX team actually done this quarter?" What's the best response?
options: Show before/after metrics: support costs down, task completion up
Show all the Figma files produced
List the number of usability tests run
Show the design system components built and the number of screens delivered
try.explain: Business impact in numbers — costs saved, revenue protected, efficiency gained — is what leadership responds to.

test.q: What is hedonic adaptation in the context of UX?
options: Users return to their baseline satisfaction
Users adapt their behavior to bad interfaces over time
Users prefer familiar designs over better ones
Users become resistant to change
test.explain: Hedonic adaptation means every improvement becomes invisible. Users don't stay grateful — they just stop noticing the old problem. (Improvements become the new normal.)

options: Because when things work smoothly, users don't notice
Because UX teams are underfunded
Because designers don't get credit in product launches
Because UX is hard to explain to non-designers
test.explain: Good UX is invisible by nature. Users notice broken things, not things that work. That invisibility IS the success. (They only notice friction.)

options: Measurements of things that stopped happening after a UX improvement
Metrics for features that are still missing from a product roadmap
Data about users who left the product
Analytics for pages users don't visit
test.explain: Absence metrics track what disappeared: fewer support tickets, lower error rates, shorter task times. They prove invisible impact.

test.q: What's the most important thing to do BEFORE shipping a UX improvement?
options: Document baseline metrics so you can show the change
Get stakeholder sign-off
Create a press release announcing the change
Run a satisfaction survey
test.explain: Without a baseline, you can't prove improvement. Document the 'before' numbers obsessively.

test.q: When communicating UX impact to leadership, which language works best?
options: Business language: cost saved, revenue retained, time recovered
Design language: improved hierarchy, better affordances
Research language: statistical significance, confidence intervals
Technical language: performance metrics, load times
test.explain: Leadership responds to business impact. Translate UX wins into costs saved, revenue protected, and efficiency gained.
